title: The true devotee
hookLine: titles mean nothing without the life that matches

cards: Someone volunteers at a shelter every Saturday, and makes sure to post a photo every time. Someone else drives an elderly neighbor to the doctor every month for years and never mentions it to anyone. Both did good.
Photos aren't wicked. But only one of the two is plainly not waiting for anything back. Ashtpadi nine has two stanzas about devotees, and both land on exactly that point.

teach.b: One stanza takes the title vaishnav, a devotee of Vishnu, an honored name. The true vaishnav, it says, is the one with whom God is well pleased, who lives apart from the pull of maya, the passing world.
Then the striking line: karam karat hovai nihkaram. Doing deeds, he remains without deeds. Nihkaram means free of the deed, free of its grip.
It doesn't mean doing nothing. It means doing the good thing without hooking yourself to the result.
The next lines say it plainly: he doesn't hanker after the fruit of any action; he is absorbed only in devotion and the singing of praise.

The next stanza takes another devotee's title, bhagauti, and says the same in a different key: the true one is dyed in love for God, leaves bad company behind, and every doubt dissolves from the mind.

Two titles, one point. Devotion is measured by the life underneath it, and especially by whether it's waiting for a reward. The neighbor who drives someone to the doctor for years isn't keeping score.
The deed is done; the doer isn't clinging. This isn't a criticism of the people who held these titles; the stanzas honor the names by asking them to be true.
It's a mirror, held up to anyone who calls themselves devoted, in any community.
Sikhs have a word for selfless service, seva, and its whole point is the same: the life, not the title.

how: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara and beyond, and read these stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib as describing devotion that seeks no reward.

o: doing good, free of the deed's grip
giving up all action to sit still
a deed done to earn a reward

games.q: the true devotee — tap the pairs.

s: nihkaram means doing nothing at all
doing deeds, yet free of them: no hankering for the fruit.
the bhagauti stanza says every doubt dissolves from the mind
dyed in love, leaving bad company behind, doubt is gone.
the true devotee in the stanza hankers after no reward
absorbed only in devotion and praise.

games.q: you've done a real good deed. nobody saw. what does the true devotee in ashtpadi nine do next?
o: post about it so it inspires others.
nothing: the deed is done, no reward sought.
games.why: karam karat hovai nihkaram: the deed is done, and the doer isn't clinging to its fruit.

practice: Choose one value you care about, kindness, honesty, patience, and picture one small act of it that no one will see, like wiping a shared table or leaving a good review for a stranger's small shop.
Notice any little wish to be noticed, and let it go on the out-breath. Breathe in: the deed; breathe out: no reward.

wordCard.voice: Nihkaram, free of the deed. Doing deeds, yet free of them, hankering after no reward.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nihkaram, free of the deed; in ashtpadi nine, doing good without clinging to the result.

carryVoice: Your line: the life, not the title. The deed is done, and the doer isn't clinging. Until tomorrow.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
